concept.name: Undertrading
concept.definition: Habitually failing to take valid trades that meet one's own criteria - hesitating, freezing, or skipping signals out of fear, recent losses, or excessive doubt. At the investor-population level its analogue is documented non-participation: the SEC-commissioned Library of Congress report describes widespread reluctance to invest at all despite suitable options.
concept.intuition: The plan says buy, the setup is there, but fear of another loss keeps the finger off the button - and the missed winners never appear in the P&L to be noticed.
concept.mechanics: Loss aversion, recent drawdowns, and performance anxiety raise the effective threshold for action, so qualifying setups are passed; because missed opportunities leave no trade record, the cost is invisible unless planned-but-skipped signals are journaled alongside executed trades.
concept.failure_modes: Chronically passing valid setups silently destroys a strategy's realized expectancy even though the visible trade record looks disciplined. The mirror failure is using patience as a rationalization for fear.
concept.misconceptions: Undertrading is not selectivity: selectivity applies criteria, undertrading violates them. Nor is every skipped signal an error - only skips driven by emotion rather than by rules.
concept.example: After three losing weeks, a trader skips the next five A-grade signals; four of them would have been winners, and his equity curve diverges from the system's backtest.

citations.source: Behavioral Patterns and Pitfalls of U.S. Investors (Library of Congress, Federal Research Division, prepared for the U.S. SEC, August 2010)
Brett N. Steenbarger, The Psychology of Trading: Tools and Techniques for Minding the Markets (Wiley, 2003) - publisher page
